doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Singing and the Nat Cole discovery
title: Stash Records and I Like Jersey Best
summary: Duo gigs with singing, the Jersey song, and the first Stash record made when Johnny Hartman fell ill.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: minutes and he’d say “sing, sing something.” And he’d say — and I’d do “Straighten Up and Fly Right,” “For Sentimental Reasons.” And then we would close out. We would do an Ellington medley and “Sing Sing Sing” or a little Goodman medley. And so as luck would have it, it’s amazing, it’s weird thinking about it because it’s so long ago to me now. In 1983, in May of ’83 I was singing this tune “I Like Jersey Best.” A buddy of mine wrote this song about our state, make a little rock & roll record with my friend singing it, because he brings me the song. A guy named Phil Bernardi brings the song to me. The guy who wrote it is Joe Cosgriff. He meets my sister at Newsweek magazine and says, “I got this song,” long story shorter, “I got this song, I want to play it for your dad,” he brings over Phil, his friend, to our house. They sit and play “I Like Jersey Best” for us. Great. We want to make a record, where can we go? Well there’s a place in Allendale, a guy had in his basement a little four track studio, we made this “I Like Jersey Best” record. That’s 1980. And I’m singing it on gigs now with Bucky. He says, “sing that Jersey song, I love that.” I sing the Jersey song, and in 1983 they want to make a record of me singing. And me and Johnny Hartman, not together, but for Stash Records. And there’s a guy named Lou Ginsberg who is a friend of my dad’s whose been following us all around, whose going to put up the money for my record. Why I don’t know, he’s just a fan, he’s got some money, he wants to hear me sing this song. So Johnny Hartman gets sick. He’s supposed to make the record, they have the studio booked and Tony Monte, a good friend of mine who was going to play piano for Johnny says “Johnny can’t do it.” He says, “He’s got a little flap in his throat, it’s not right.” So Bernie Brightman calls and says, “I’ve got studio time on Wednesday. So why don’t you bring him in and we’ll make the record right away.” So like this is Monday. So I’m going okay we’ll do “Route 66,” “Straighten Up and Fly Right,” “Sentimental Reasons.” I also had found Dave Frishberg so I learned “I’m Hip.” And my father had some old scratchy Joe Mooney records so I did “Man with a Million Dollars,” and “Have Another One Not Me,” and “I Like Jersey Best.” So I go in the studio, I sit in the booth, there’s Russ Kassoff on piano, Jerry Bruno on bass and my father, the Pierre Trio, the Pierre Hotel trio where he was working. And they accompany me and I sing and it comes out and they had a big party and Peggy Lee came to the party and it was this really wild scene. And WNEW here in town starts playing the record and now all of a sudden I’m on the radio and I’m a vocalist. It wasn’t any conscious effort to say be a singer, it was just part of what I was doing to make a living. I was singing and playing in bars, or in restaurants. And so — I’m doing the right thing, like talking about this, right?
